analysis.one_liner: Overhauls how Medicare pays private Medicare Advantage plans and changes how seniors are enrolled in them.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: introduced in May 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to two committees, it never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change Medicare Advantage, the private plans that cover most people on Medicare. Starting in 2028, plans would have to pay providers through a fixed per-patient arrangement rather than fee-for-service, government payment benchmarks would be cut to 75% of the blended benchmark, and plans could no longer boost payments by collecting diagnoses from chart reviews and health risk assessments — a practice critics say inflates costs. It would also auto-enroll new Medicare beneficiaries into the lowest-premium private plan, lock them in for three years, require hospice to be covered inside these plans, and create a new exception to the physician self-referral law for equipment and drugs under these plans.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, taxpayers would benefit from lower Medicare Advantage payments (MA overpayment estimates run in the tens of billions per year), and beneficiaries auto-enrolled into the lowest-premium plan would pay less out of pocket. Doctors could also refer patients for medical equipment and drugs under MA plans without violating the self-referral ban.

how_it_helps.text: It ends the practice of counting diagnoses collected through chart reviews and stand-alone health risk assessments when setting MA payments, and limits health-status risk adjustment to diagnoses documented on claims from actual visits over a two-year lookback — directly targeting the coding practices that MedPAC and federal watchdogs have identified as inflating MA payments [S2].
It cuts the payment benchmark for most MA plans to 75% of the blended benchmark beginning in 2028 and eliminates quality-bonus payment increases, reducing what the government pays private plans [S2].
It auto-enrolls new Medicare beneficiaries into the lowest-premium MA plan available to them, which by design lowers what enrollees pay in premiums [S2].
It lets the Secretary create stop-loss payments for plans facing unusually high expenditures, and requires hospice care to be covered inside MA plans rather than carved out [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurance companies would bear the cost through lower benchmarks and coding restrictions. Some beneficiaries would lose flexibility: they would be defaulted into an MA plan and unable to switch plans or return to traditional Medicare for three years, and a new self-referral exception could expose patients to physician-owned equipment and drug arrangements.
analysis.who_pays_short: MA insurers and some seniors' plan choice

drawbacks.text: Automatic enrollment would place every new Medicare beneficiary into the lowest-premium private MA plan by default, and once enrolled they could not switch plans or return to traditional Medicare for three years except in hardship cases — removing a choice seniors currently make freely every year [S2].

The bill removes the current-law protection that keeps hospice care outside MA, so terminally ill beneficiaries would receive hospice through their private plan rather than under traditional Medicare rules [S2].

It adds a new self-referral exception allowing physicians to refer Medicare patients for durable medical equipment and Part D drugs under MA plans without violating the physician self-referral (Stark) law [S2].

The mandated payment cuts take effect on a fixed date (2028) regardless of market readiness; a stop-loss mechanism to cushion plans facing unusually high costs is discretionary ('may establish') and must be implemented budget-neutrally, so the risk of plan exits or benefit cuts in affected areas is not fully addressed in the text [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost-control pieces are the bill's real substance: capping plan benchmarks at 75% of the blended benchmark, banning chart-review and health-risk-assessment diagnoses in risk adjustment, and ending quality bonus increases are the kind of changes MedPAC and others have long suggested because MA coding has cost taxpayers tens of billions of dollars a year [S2]. But the bill buys that savings with a radical change for beneficiaries: automatic enrollment into the lowest-premium MA plan, a three-year lock-in, and the removal of the traditional Medicare hospice carve-out [S2]. Weighing an estimated 32 million beneficiaries' flexibility against taxpayer savings, the trade is real but the bill as written asks the most vulnerable population in the health system to bear the adjustment risk, and the automatic-enrollment design (defaulting into the cheapest plan rather than into traditional Medicare) is a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 15, 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees the same day [S4].
The only subsequent activity was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on June 3, 2025; neither committee has taken it up [S4].
Even if it moved, its provisions would not take effect until 2028, so its real-world effects remain hypothetical [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet — the bill has not advanced, so current Medicare Advantage payment rules remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill is stalled

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1][S2].

sides.party_line_note: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes or committee action, there is no record of who supports or opposes the bill.

industries.note: The bill cuts payment benchmarks to 75%, bans chart-review and risk-assessment diagnoses from risk adjustment, and ends quality bonus increases — closing coding channels that have driven MA overpayments. Beneficiaries would also be defaulted into low-premium MA plans, giving insurers a captive enrollment base even as their payments shrink.

industries.industry: Traditional Medicare providers (hospitals and physicians paid fee-for-service)
industries.note: Requiring capitated payment and moving hospice into MA plans shrinks the volume of care delivered under traditional fee-for-service Medicare, reducing revenue for providers who bill Medicare directly.

industries.industry: Durable medical equipment suppliers and pharmacy intermediaries under MA
industries.note: A new exception to the physician self-referral (Stark) law would let physicians refer MA patients for durable medical equipment and Part D drugs in which they have a financial interest, loosening an anti-kickback-style safeguard.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced without cosponsors and referred to two committees without a hearing almost never advance. Unless Schweikert builds cosponsor support or the provisions are folded into a larger Medicare package, the bill will die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
